events.title: ASCII standard published
events.summary: The American National Standards Institute adopted [ASCII] as ANSI X3.4-1963 — a 7-bit character encoding for information interchange.
events.about: [ASCII] gave computers a shared alphabet for text files, terminals, and protocols. Every later encoding — including [UTF-8] — builds on or maps through [ASCII]'s 128 code points, making it the invisible layer beneath email, [HTTP], [JSON], and source code.

narrative.whyChosen: [ASCII] became the universal text layer for hardware and software from the 1960s onward.
narrative.whyImportant: A single character set let programs and networks exchange plain text without vendor-specific codes.
narrative.problemSolved: Each manufacturer used incompatible [teletype] and punch-card character sets.

events.title: Ivan Sutherland creates Sketchpad
events.summary: Ivan Sutherland demonstrated Sketchpad in 1963 — the first program to use a light pen for interactive drawing, constraints, and zoom on a computer display.
events.about: Sketchpad on [MIT]'s TX-2 pioneered direct manipulation, object instances, and constraint solving — ideas that became CAD, GUIs, and modern graphics toolkits. Sutherland's PhD work showed computers could be visual design instruments, not just number crunchers.

narrative.whyChosen: Sketchpad invented interactive computer graphics and constraint-based drawing.
narrative.whyImportant: It foreshadowed CAD, [WYSIWYG] editors, and graphical user interfaces decades ahead.
narrative.problemSolved: Engineers drafted on paper with no way to edit geometry or reuse symbols interactively on screen.
